findings.title: Replay protection exists for one of four message types; cancel, reissue and refund are unbounded repeat primitives
findings.class: Business-logic abuse / missing idempotency (CWE-837)
findings.evidence: Only handle_payout consults the store: handlers.py:81-82 `cached = idempotency.lookup(key); if cached:`. handle_payout_cancel (handlers.py:91) credits an arbitrary account unconditionally: handlers.py:94-99 `amount = int(msg['amount_cents']); ledger.post_entry(LedgerEntry(tenant_id=msg['tenant_id'], account=msg['destination_account'], amount_cents=amount, ...))` — positive, a credit, with no reference to any prior payout. handle_payout_reissue calls remember at handlers.py:110 but never lookup. handle_refund has neither. Even the one protection expires: settings.py:52 idempotency_ttl_seconds default 86400.
findings.impact: payout.cancel is a mint: one payouts:write actor — or, via the envelope defect, anyone who can re-label a signed entry — credits any well-formed account any amount, repeatedly, with no matching payout required and no cap. refund debits the clearing account the same way. Nothing in the message binds a cancel to a payout that happened.
findings.recommendation: Make idempotency a property of the dispatch loop, not of one handler: claim the key in process() before the handler runs, for every type. Require cancel and refund to name the original idempotency_key, verify a settled receipt exists for it, and verify the amount does not exceed what was settled.

triage.reason: No unique constraint exists; the journal insert at ledger.py:78 has no conflict clause and the Redis balance is a plain SET.
The effect is a committed ledger movement, not a cosmetic one.
The gap is per-handler and all three ungated handlers are registered at consumer.py:28-30.

scope.established_by: cross-listed all four handlers against every call of idempotency.lookup/remember: three call sites covering two handlers

findings.title: The idempotency check is a read-decide-write with no atomicity, and the atomic primitive that would fix it has zero callers
findings.class: Race condition / TOCTOU (CWE-367)
findings.evidence: handlers.py:80-87 reads (`cached = idempotency.lookup(key)`), decides, moves the money (`receipt = _apply_payout(msg)`) and only then writes (`idempotency.remember(key, receipt)`). The correct primitive is written one module away and never used: idempotency.py:42-44 `def claim(idempotency_key) -> bool: return bool(_redis().set(slot(idempotency_key), '{}', nx=True, ex=300))`. `grep -rn 'claim(\|release('` over the package returns exactly one hit each — the definitions.
findings.impact: Two deliveries of the same idempotency_key — the redelivery the module's own docstring says it exists to absorb — land on two consumers in the group, both read None, and both apply. Double spend. The window is the whole of _apply_payout: two Redis round trips, a Postgres insert and a 3-second HTTP call. A crash between the apply and the remember produces the same result on the next delivery with no concurrency at all.
findings.recommendation: Replace the sequence with claim() -> apply -> remember() -> release() on failure, so the slot is taken before the money moves; add a unique index on (tenant_id, reference) in settlement.journal as the backstop that does not depend on Redis being available.

triage.reason: No lock, no unique constraint and no conditional update anywhere on the path; the journal insert at ledger.py:78-83 is an unconditional insert.
No database schema in scope declares a constraint; had one been claimed without the artifact this would be UNKNOWN.
lookup/remember are ordinary GET/SET (idempotency.py:30, :35), not an atomic pair.

scope.established_by: symbol-count of claim/release across the package plus reading the only read-decide-write sequence guarding a money movement

findings.title: The payout amount is bounded only on the publish path; the consume path accepts any integer, including negative
findings.class: Missing input validation on the trust boundary; declared limit with no reader on the reachable path (CWE-20, CWE-1284)
findings.evidence: The cap exists with one reader: schemas.py:18 `MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS = 5_000_000` and schemas.py:27 `amount_cents: int = Field(gt=0, le=MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS)` on PayoutRequest. `grep -rn PayoutRequest` returns schemas.py:21, consumer.py:21 (import), consumer.py:44 and consumer.py:54 — both inside publish_payout. What the consumer produces is an unvalidated dict: consumer.py:74 `msg = json.loads(body)`. The model that is re-validated declares no bound: schemas.py:41 `amount_cents: int` with no Field. handlers.py:44 `amount = int(msg['amount_cents'])`.
findings.impact: Two escapes. The $50,000 ceiling is absent wherever untrusted input actually arrives. And gt=0 is absent too: a negative amount_cents inverts the double entry — handlers.py:46-54 posts -amount (a debit) to CLEARING_ACCOUNT and handlers.py:55-63 posts -(-amount) (a credit) to the attacker-named destination. A payout message with amount_cents: -500000 credits the destination and drains the clearing account, bounded only by the clearing balance.
findings.recommendation: Validate in decode(): parse the body with PayoutRequest.model_validate (and a per-type model for cancel/reissue/refund) before it reaches any handler, and fail closed on ValidationError without dead-lettering. Put the domain bounds on LedgerEntry.amount_cents too, since that is the model the ledger writer receives.

triage.reason: The only re-validation on the consume path is LedgerEntry, which constrains tenant_id, account, currency and reference and deliberately not amount_cents.
msg['amount_cents'] originates in the stream body.
The impact is a committed balance change.
Checked whether PayoutRequest narrows the reachable path; it does the opposite, sitting only on the publish side that untrusted input does not traverse.

scope.established_by: counted readers of MAX_PAYOUT_CENTS (one) and of PayoutRequest (publish-side only), then read every int(msg['amount_cents'])

findings.title: The check that a destination belongs to the tenant runs only where the data is already trusted
findings.class: Broken object-level authorization / cross-tenant object reference (CWE-639)
findings.evidence: The ownership check exists with a database query behind it: consumer.py:44-49 `_destination_is_registered` selects from settlement.tenant_accounts where tenant_id and account match and status = 'active'. It has exactly one caller, on the producing side: consumer.py:57. On the consuming side msg['destination_account'] reaches the ledger with only a shape check (AccountRef, schemas.py:15): handlers.py:58 and handlers.py:98. `grep -rn _destination_is_registered` returns two hits, both in consumer.py.
findings.impact: The tenant_accounts table is the authority on who may receive a tenant's money and is never consulted where untrusted input arrives. Any message names any account matching the AccountRef regex — another tenant's account, a closed account, one with status != 'active' — and the movement is applied. handle_payout_cancel makes it a write primitive against a foreign account rather than merely a misdirected payout.
findings.recommendation: Move _destination_is_registered into the handler path (or into decode) and run it against (msg['tenant_id'], msg['destination_account']) for every type that names an account. Keep the publish-side call as defence in depth; the authoritative one must be on the consume side.

triage.reason: The only control between the message and the ledger is the AccountRef regex, which constrains the format of the name, not who owns it.
Nothing in scope bounds the exposure; tenant_accounts exists precisely to bound it and is not queried here.
The named row is a settlement account; naming it moves money into or out of it.
Checked whether publish_payout is on the path to the handlers: it is not — consumer.py:54 is a separate entry point and process (consumer.py:87) never calls it.

scope.established_by: counted callers of _destination_is_registered and listed every place destination_account reaches a LedgerEntry

findings.title: Currency is validated and then discarded: one balance counter per account holds USD, EUR and GBP together
findings.class: Money-handling invariant violation (CWE-682)
findings.evidence: ledger.py:35-36 `def balance_key(tenant_id, account): return f'balance:{tenant_id}:{account}'` — no currency component. The arithmetic ignores entry.currency entirely: ledger.py:63-64 `current = int(pipe.get(key) or 0); new_balance = current + entry.amount_cents`. Currency is carried to the journal at ledger.py:82 and nowhere else. Reconciliation simply asserts one: reconcile.py:63 passes the literal 'USD'.
findings.impact: LedgerEntry.currency (schemas.py:42) is a Literal['USD','EUR','GBP'] — carefully validated, then unused in the only place it matters. Because msg['currency'] is attacker-chosen on the consume path, an actor credits an account in the weakest currency and debits it in the strongest against the same counter: the overdraw guard at ledger.py:65 is satisfied throughout and value is created out of the exchange-rate difference. Any multi-currency account can also never reconcile.
findings.recommendation: Make currency part of the account's identity: balance:{tenant_id}:{account}:{currency}, and refuse any LedgerEntry whose currency differs from the account's registered currency. Take the reconciliation currency from the statement or the account record instead of the literal.

triage.reason: No layer separates currencies; post_entry is the only writer of the balance and uses balance_key unchanged.
msg['currency'] comes from the stream (handlers.py:51, :60, :100, :123).
Checked whether the Literal constraint implies single-currency accounts elsewhere; nothing in scope binds an account to a currency.

scope.established_by: traced every reader of balance_key (ledger.py:40, ledger.py:57, reconcile.py:56) and every use of entry.currency

findings.title: A payout's two movements are not atomic, and a partial application is replayed from the top
findings.class: Improper handling of partial failure / non-atomic transaction (CWE-754, CWE-362)
findings.evidence: Two independent commits with no transaction spanning them: handlers.py:46 posts leg 1 (credit CLEARING_ACCOUNT, committing at ledger.py:72) and handlers.py:55 posts leg 2 (debit the destination), which may raise at ledger.py:65-67 `if new_balance < 0: raise InsufficientFunds`. Inside a single leg the Redis balance and the Postgres journal are two separate commits against two separate stores: ledger.py:71-72 `pipe.set(key, new_balance); pipe.execute()` then ledger.py:77 `with psycopg.connect(...)`.
findings.impact: When leg 2 fails the clearing credit stands and the exception propagates to consumer.py:114, which dead-letters the entry. The replay path re-enters _apply_payout from the top and credits the clearing account again. Every failed attempt inflates the clearing account by the payout amount, permanently and without limit, and the journal accumulates unmatched half-entries. The journal is written at ledger.py:78 and reconcile.py:59 and never read back, so the audit trail cannot reconstruct the truth.
findings.recommendation: Write both legs in one Postgres transaction with a unique (tenant_id, reference, account) constraint, and derive the Redis balance from it as a cache rather than as the source of truth. At minimum make replay idempotent per leg so re-entry cannot re-credit.

triage.reason: psycopg.connect as a context manager commits per call (ledger.py:77, reconcile.py:58); there is no outer transaction and no compensating reversal anywhere in the package.
The failure is triggerable by a message that names an underfunded destination.
The inconsistency is durable and self-amplifying under the service's own retry design.

scope.established_by: traced the commit points of both stores and the re-entry point of the replay path

findings.title: Reconciliation overwrites balances from an unvalidated CSV, bypassing the overdraw guard entirely
findings.class: Missing authorization and input validation on a privileged write path (CWE-20, CWE-862)
findings.evidence: reconcile.py:56 `_redis().set(balance_key(d.tenant_id, d.account), d.theirs_cents)` — the balance is set, not posted, so ledger.post_entry and its guard are not on this path. The values come straight from the file: reconcile.py:44-47 `for row in csv.DictReader(fh): tenant_id = row['tenant_id']; account = row['account']; theirs = int(row['closing_cents'])` — no TenantId pattern, no AccountRef pattern, no sign or magnitude bound. Compare the guard this path skips: ledger.py:65.
findings.impact: The statement file is a set-any-balance-to-any-value primitive: no scope check, no signature check, no bound on magnitude or sign, no pattern check on tenant or account — a row naming an account that does not exist simply creates the key. Negative closing positions are accepted, so the overdraw invariant is broken from outside. int() raising on a malformed row aborts run() partway with earlier adjustments committed and no rollback. Inference not closed: whether an upstream job authenticates the file before invoking run().
findings.recommendation: Validate every row against a pydantic model reusing TenantId/AccountRef and a signed magnitude bound; require the statement to be authenticated before a single row is applied; and apply adjustments through ledger.post_entry inside one transaction so a bad row rolls the batch back.

triage.reason: apply_adjustment calls redis.set directly; the post_entry guard is not reachable from this path.
The values originate in an external party's file.
The scheme is a distinct principal; __init__.py:4-5 lists the reconciliation job as a stream producer alongside two other services.
Whether an upstream job authenticates the file before invoking run() cannot be established from this tree. Caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: read the full path from read_statement to the Redis write and compared it against ledger.post_entry's guard

findings.title: max_delivery_attempts is declared, documented and read by nothing; the first failure dead-letters
findings.class: Declared limit with no enforcement (CWE-1188, CWE-754)
findings.evidence: `grep -rn max_delivery_attempts` over the package returns exactly two lines and one is prose: settings.py:51 the declaration, consumer.py:5 a docstring describing the policy. What the code does on the first exception of any kind: consumer.py:114-117 `except Exception: r.xadd(settings.dead_letter_stream, ...); r.xack(settings.stream, settings.group, entry_id)`.
findings.impact: No retry policy exists. A single transient Postgres timeout — the cause retry.py:3-4 names as almost always — sends a live payout straight to the DLQ, where the replay path has no controls. The dead setting is what turns ordinary infrastructure flapping into traffic on the unauthenticated replay path. The xack also empties the Redis pending-entries list, so the stream's own at-least-once redelivery cannot help.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the documented policy — track delivery count via XPENDING/XAUTOCLAIM and dead-letter only past max_delivery_attempts — or delete the setting and the docstring. Separate transient failures from permanent rejections: a bad signature and a Forbidden must never be retried at all.

triage.reason: The question is not whether the path ships but whether the limit is read; it is not.
No external component consumes this value; the reader search was over the whole package and the only non-declaration hit is a docstring.
Settings is a plain frozen dataclass instantiated once at settings.py:55, so a symbol search is complete for it.

scope.established_by: symbol count of max_delivery_attempts across the package (two, one a docstring), cross-checked against the other four _int settings, all of which do have real readers

findings.title: Settlement receipts POSTed over plaintext HTTP with redirects followed automatically
findings.class: Cleartext transmission of sensitive data; uncontrolled redirect forwarding (CWE-319, CWE-441)
findings.evidence: handlers.py:37 `httpx.post(hook_url, json=payload, timeout=3.0, follow_redirects=True)` with a plaintext default target at settings.py:45-46 `notify_url: str = os.getenv('NOTIFY_URL', 'http://notifications.internal.fieldops/hooks/settlement')`. The payload is the full financial receipt: handlers.py:65-73 carries tenant_id, destination_account, amount_cents and balance_after.
findings.impact: Tenant identifiers, destination account references, amounts and running balances cross the network unencrypted and unauthenticated. Because follow_redirects=True and httpx preserves method and body on 307/308, whoever controls or can spoof the internal hostname over that plaintext channel redirects every receipt to an arbitrary host, with no allowlist on the final URL. Inference not closed: whether a mandatory egress proxy or service mesh enforces TLS.
findings.recommendation: Use https with certificate verification; set follow_redirects=False on a fire-and-forget hook that ignores its response anyway; if redirects must be followed, validate the final URL against an allowlist after resolution. Consider whether balance_after needs to leave the service at all.

triage.reason: For the URL origin only: hook_url is settings.notify_url, a configuration constant, never a message field (handlers.py:73 is its only caller). This is why the finding is scoped to transport and redirect handling and not reported as SSRF.
An internal hostname is not a bound; nothing in scope restricts egress.
Account references, amounts and balances are financial records.
A mandatory egress proxy enforcing TLS would change this; no such artifact is in scope.

scope.established_by: single caller of _notify (handlers.py:73) and the only httpx call in the package
scope.narrowed_by: settlement-worker/settlement/handlers.py:73 — reached only from _apply_payout, so payout and reissue receipts; cancel and refund do not notify.

findings.title: The journal reference is interpolated into SQL by f-string while its four neighbours are bound
findings.class: SQL construction by interpolation (CWE-89)
findings.evidence: ledger.py:78-83: four parameters bound, the fifth spliced in — `"insert into settlement.journal (tenant_id, account, amount_cents, currency, reference) " f"values (%s, %s, %s, %s, '{entry.reference}')"` with the tuple carrying only the first four. The sibling insert two files away does it correctly: reconcile.py:62 uses five placeholders with all five in the tuple at :63.
findings.impact: Not exploitable today: entry.reference is typed Reference (schemas.py:16, ^[A-Za-z0-9:_.\-]{1,64}$), which admits no quote, and all four in-tree construction sites go through full LedgerEntry validation. What is absent is the defence, not the exploit: the sink's safety rests entirely on a pattern declared in another module and applied only at construction time. pydantic v2 does not validate on assignment by default and model_construct skips validation, so a future caller turns line 81 into injection with no change to this file.
findings.recommendation: Bind it — move entry.reference into the parameter tuple and make the fifth placeholder %s. Separately, pyproject.toml:18-20 configures ruff with line-length and target-version only, so S608 never runs; add the flake8-bandit rule set.

triage.reason: The constraint is not enforced in a layer that cannot be skipped: it is applied at construction, and post_entry's LedgerEntry annotation is a hint Python does not enforce.

The value is constrained by an allowlist before it reaches the sink: settlement-worker/settlement/schemas.py:16 Reference is applied at every LedgerEntry construction and admits no quote. This keeps the finding out of confirmed and out of critical.
Real but bounded to a hardening item; the finding is written down and the severity drops.

scope.established_by: enumerated every execute in the package (consumer.py:46, ledger.py:47, ledger.py:78, reconcile.py:59) and every LedgerEntry construction (four); line 81 is the only interpolated one
scope.narrowed_by: settlement-worker/settlement/schemas.py:16 — the Reference pattern is the sole reason this is not exploitable today.

findings.title: Statement fields reach a line-oriented log without neutralisation
findings.class: Log injection (CWE-117)
findings.evidence: Flagged UNCLEARED by log_escaper.py (reconcile.py:70, arg1/arg2/arg3 Attribute). reconcile.py:70-72 `log.info('adjusting %s/%s by %d cents', d.tenant_id, d.account, d.delta)` — values trace to Discrepancy at reconcile.py:50, built from row['tenant_id'] and row['account'] at :45-46, from csv.DictReader at :44. A quoted CSV field preserves \r\n verbatim, and the only formatter configured in the package is logging.basicConfig (consumer.py:122, retry.py:65), i.e. BASIC_FORMAT.
findings.impact: One statement row forges arbitrary additional log records — including fabricated adjustment lines for accounts that were never touched, which is precisely the record a finance team would use to reconstruct a disputed reconciliation. No execution, so this is an accountability loss rather than a code-execution path.
findings.recommendation: Validate tenant_id/account against the existing TenantId/AccountRef patterns before use, and emit one JSON object per event rather than a formatted line.

triage.reason: No allowlist or pattern is applied between csv.DictReader and the logging call.
The sink is line-oriented text under BASIC_FORMAT; a newline forges a record.
%s deferred interpolation is not an escaper.
No consumer in scope executes or renders the log, so the severity is low rather than higher; the finding is written down.

scope.established_by: log_escaper.py enumeration (ten calls, two uncleared) plus manual back-tracing of both flagged sites

findings.title: Every money-movement log line loses its identifying fields, while exception text keeps account and actor references
findings.class: Insufficient logging of security-relevant events; sensitive data in traceback (CWE-778, CWE-532)
findings.evidence: consumer.py:122 `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)` installs BASIC_FORMAT (%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s), which renders no extra attribute — so every structured field attached below is dropped: consumer.py:91, :96, :115, handlers.py:39, handlers.py:83, retry.py:39, retry.py:45 all pass extra={...}. The declared structured logger is never wired: pyproject.toml:11 declares structlog and `grep -rn structlog` over the package returns zero hits. Meanwhile log.exception does render exc_info, so the traceback carries ledger.py:68 f'{entry.account} would go to {new_balance}' and handlers.py:31 f"{msg['actor_id']} lacks {scope}".
findings.impact: Every settled payout logs the literal string 'INFO:settlement.consumer:handled' with no entry id, no type and no receipt — the forensic record of money movement does not exist, and DLQ traffic is equally unattributable. At the same time the one channel that does render is the uncurated one, emitting account references and actor identifiers with no redaction. The project believes it has structured logging because the dependency is declared and every call site passes extra.
findings.recommendation: Configure the declared structlog (or a Formatter naming the fields) so extra is emitted as JSON; add a redaction processor for account and actor fields; replace log.exception on rejection paths with an explicit curated event so the traceback is not the audit trail.

triage.reason: For the disclosure half — account and actor references are the identifiers of financial records.
There is no logging.conf, no dictConfig and no other basicConfig in the package; the two that exist both take the default format.
No external principal reaches these logs from within scope, so this stays low.

scope.established_by: log_escaper.py call enumeration (ten sites) cross-referenced against every basicConfig and a package-wide structlog search

findings.title: The configured test path does not exist, so the declared test gate collects nothing
findings.class: Control declared with nothing behind it (CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: pyproject.toml:22-23 `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` / `testpaths = ["tests"]`. `ls settlement-worker/tests` returns No such file or directory and `find settlement-worker -name 'test*'` is empty. The package ships nine .py files, none of them tests.
findings.impact: A service that moves money has no automated verification of any invariant — not the overdraw guard, not idempotency, not signature verification. pytest collects zero items and exits 5, which many CI configurations treat as a non-failure, so the gate reports green while testing nothing.
findings.recommendation: Create tests/ with negative tests for the controls this report shows to be absent or inert; fail the build on zero collected tests.

triage.reason: The configuration ships as written.
Tests may live in a parent repository outside the assigned scope; the directory the manifest itself names does not exist, which is the assertion made here.
Process defect, not a reachable vulnerability; severity low.

scope.established_by: COV-02 key-by-key manifest enumeration plus a directory listing

findings.title: _legacy_reprocess is an unreferenced, unauthenticated apply path kept past its own stated expiry
findings.class: Dead code on a privileged path (CWE-561, CWE-862)
findings.evidence: retry.py:54-61 promotes the entire stream entry to a message — `msg = {k: v for k, v in entry.items() if k not in {'origin_id','sig'}}` — and hands it to `handlers._apply_payout(msg)`, the function whose contract is 'assumes the caller has already authorised the message'. `grep -rn _legacy_reprocess` over the package returns one hit, the definition. The docstring's claim that the last flattened entry aged out in March is target data; what is established is that the function has no caller.
findings.impact: The attacker would control every key except origin_id and sig, which are the only two removed. Unreachable today, so it is a hardening item; but it is a loaded path in a money service whose stated reason to exist has expired, and a single future call site makes it the dead-letter bypass with no signature check even nominally in the picture.
findings.recommendation: Delete it. If a flattened-entry migration is ever needed again, write it against the authenticated handle_* dispatch.

triage.reason: Were it called, nothing on its path authenticates or authorizes.

The path does not execute in what ships: zero callers in the package. This caps the finding at a hardening note; per FP-10 it is still written down, because the code is present in the shipped module and one line makes it live.

scope.established_by: symbol search across the package
scope.narrowed_by: zero callers — the function is defined and never invoked.

findings.title: The stream body is parsed with no size or type constraint and then indexed as a dict
findings.class: Unconstrained input parsing (CWE-400, CWE-20)
findings.evidence: consumer.py:67 `body = entry.get('body','{}')`, consumer.py:74 `msg = json.loads(body)` with no size cap and no type assertion, consumer.py:75 then indexes it. Same shape at retry.py:25. Nothing between the stream read (consumer.py:101-107) and the parse bounds the entry: settings.read_batch defaults to 64 entries per call with no byte budget.
findings.impact: A Redis stream field may hold up to 512 MB; json.loads materialises it, and read_batch allows 64 such entries per XREADGROUP call, so a worker's memory is bounded by what a publisher chooses rather than by configuration. If the body parses to a non-dict, line 75 raises TypeError, which run_once converts into a dead-letter — a cheap way to fill the DLQ that is the unauthenticated way back in. Inference not closed: a broker-side entry-size limit would bound the allocation.
findings.recommendation: Reject bodies over a configured byte limit before parsing, assert isinstance(msg, dict) immediately after the parse, and give read_batch a companion byte budget.

triage.reason: There is no check at all before the allocation.
body is the attacker-supplied stream field.
The publisher is the second principal named in the trust boundary.
A broker-side size limit would bound the allocation; no such configuration is in scope. This is why the status is probable.

scope.established_by: enumerated both json.loads sites in the package

findings.title: The optimistic-lock retry loop has no attempt bound
findings.class: Unbounded retry / livelock (CWE-834)
findings.evidence: ledger.py:60-75 `while True: try: pipe.watch(key) ... except redis.WatchError: continue` — no attempt counter, no backoff, no ceiling. redis.Redis.from_url at ledger.py:32 sets no socket timeout either.
findings.impact: The WATCH/MULTI pattern is correct; what is missing is a ceiling. Under sustained contention on one hot balance key — a shared CLEARING_ACCOUNT that every payout and refund touches by construction — a worker can spin indefinitely, holding its Redis connection and its consumer-group entry, with no log line and no metric. Self-inflicted availability risk that grows with worker count. Inference not closed: the observed retry distribution at realistic worker concurrency was not measured.
findings.recommendation: Bound the loop (e.g. eight attempts with jittered backoff), raise a distinct exception on exhaustion, and reconsider routing every movement through one clearing key.

triage.reason: No timeout, deadline or attempt cap on the path.
Partially: the contention is generated by the service's own workers rather than by a second principal, which is what keeps this low and probable.

scope.established_by: read the only optimistic-lock loop in the package

findings.title: Configuration errors degrade silently to defaults instead of failing at startup
findings.class: Fail-open configuration (CWE-1188, CWE-703)
findings.evidence: settings.py:9-16 `def _int(name, default): raw = os.getenv(name); if not raw: return default; try: return int(raw) except ValueError: return default` — a typo becomes the default, silently. No bound is applied either: negative and zero values pass straight through for all four callers (settings.py:49, :50, :51, :52).
findings.impact: MAX_DELIVERY_ATTEMPTS=5x becomes 5, IDEMPOTENCY_TTL=1d becomes 86400, and nothing is logged. An operator who believes they have tightened a limit has not, with no signal. IDEMPOTENCY_TTL=0 passes the truthiness check and reaches idempotency.py:38 as ex=0, which Redis rejects at runtime rather than at startup.
findings.recommendation: Raise on an unparseable value, validate ranges per setting, and log the resolved configuration once at startup so the effective values are observable.

triage.reason: This is the shipped configuration loader, executed at import (settings.py:55).
No direct attacker path; bounded to a hardening item at low severity.

scope.established_by: key-by-key enumeration of settings.py per COV-02

findings.title: A task role in the SERVICES list has no policy entry and silently receives Action:'*' Resource:'*'
findings.class: Privilege escalation / over-permissive IAM (CWE-284, CWE-269)
findings.evidence: iam.ts:45-47 `const BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS: Statement[] = [{ Effect: 'Allow', Action: '*', Resource: '*' }]`. iam.ts:50-55 SERVICES lists four services including 'settlement-worker'. iam.ts:80 `const statements = SERVICE_POLICIES[service] ?? BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS`. SERVICE_POLICIES (iam.ts:15-42) has exactly three keys: fieldops-api, reports-renderer, warehouse-loader. `grep -rn "settlement-worker"` returns one hit, iam.ts:54. The lookup returns undefined and ?? selects the bootstrap statement, attached at iam.ts:82-85.
findings.impact: The settlement worker's ECS task role is an account administrator in both stacks. Any code execution in that container — a dependency compromise, an SSRF reaching the task metadata endpoint — yields full control of the AWS account: read every bucket, create IAM users, disable logging, snapshot and exfiltrate the Postgres primary. The comment at iam.ts:44 is an admission of temporary intent, not a bound, and it is data, not authorization.
findings.recommendation: Delete BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS. Replace `?? BOOTSTRAP_STATEMENTS` with a build-time failure, add the real settlement-worker statement set, and attach a permissions boundary to every role created in this loop.

triage.reason: No SCP, permissions boundary or organization guardrail is declared anywhere in this tree; grep for boundary/SCP returns nothing.
iam.ts:44 states intent ('until a workload's real permission set has been worked out') but names no bound. Intent is not a bound.
Action:'*' Resource:'*' with no Condition key; the statement applies to the entire account for the whole life of the role.

scope.established_by: SERVICES list at iam.ts:50-55 subtracted from SERVICE_POLICIES keys at iam.ts:16,28,35; the loop at iam.ts:65 runs once per service in every stack, so this is one RolePolicy in prod and one in staging

findings.title: Staging exports bucket has all four public-access-block protections disabled and a declared anonymous read policy, while production export objects are replicated into it
findings.class: Sensitive data exposure / public object storage (CWE-668, CWE-552)
findings.evidence: Pulumi.staging.yaml:9 `publicExports: "true"` and :12 `replicateProdExports: "true"`, read at index.ts:13-14 and consumed at storage.ts:42-48, where all four flags are `!args.publicExports` — blockPublicAcls, blockPublicPolicy, ignorePublicAcls and restrictPublicBuckets all become false. storage.ts:58-62 declares `Sid: 'ReadExports', Principal:'*', Action:['s3:GetObject'], Resource: `${arn}/*``. storage.ts:82-84 grants a cross-account role s3:ReplicateObject, s3:ReplicateDelete and s3:ReplicateTags. The bucket is tagged at storage.ts:29 `Contains: 'work-order-and-billing-exports'`.
findings.impact: One boolean inverts four independent protections at once. Anyone who can enumerate or guess the bucket name reads customer billing exports without credentials, and Pulumi.staging.yaml:11-12 states the intent to keep staging loaded with the same shape of data partners see in prod. s3:ReplicateDelete additionally lets the source account delete objects here. Qualifier: the anonymous policy and the replication policy are two BucketPolicy resources on the same bucket and AWS permits only one, so either staging is world-readable or prod replication works; the code does not determine which and both branches are defects. The PAB is unconditional and open in staging regardless.
findings.recommendation: Delete the publicExports flag and the anonymous policy block; serve exports through the existing CloudFront distribution with an Origin Access Control, as the reports bucket already does. Hard-code all four PAB flags to true on every bucket. Set replicateProdExports to false in staging or replicate a synthetic dataset.

triage.reason: Pulumi.staging.yaml:7-8 asserts the exposure is intended ('leave the objects readable') but names no bound — no prefix restriction, no aws:SourceVpce condition, no requester allowlist. Per FP-05 the finding moves to what sits behind it, which is prod billing data.
storage.ts:29 tags the bucket Contains: 'work-order-and-billing-exports' — the repository itself classifies the content as billing records.
An account-level public access block could override the bucket-level one, but no exported artifact or written statement exists in this tree. Per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.
Resource is `${arn}/*` — every object, no prefix narrowing.

scope.established_by: publicExports/replicateProdExports read at index.ts:13-14, passed at index.ts:47-48, consumed at storage.ts:44-47/50/70; both flags are "true" only in Pulumi.staging.yaml:9,12
scope.narrowed_by: pulumi-platform/Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8 — both flags are "false" in prod, so the prod PAB is fully closed and neither policy resource is created. This finding is staging-only.

findings.title: Postgres port 5432 opened to 0.0.0.0/0, and the analytics read replica is publiclyAccessible in the public subnets
findings.class: Network exposure of a datastore (CWE-1327, CWE-284)
findings.evidence: data.ts:71-78 creates a SecurityGroupIngressRule on network.dbSecurityGroup for tcp 5432 with `cidrIpv4: '0.0.0.0/0'`, justified by a comment at data.ts:69-70 that the BI vendor rotates its egress addresses weekly. data.ts:54-57 places replicaSubnets in network.publicSubnetIds; data.ts:62-64 sets that subnet group, the same security group and `publiclyAccessible: true`. network.ts:30-33 gives the public route table a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway and network.ts:53-56 associates the public subnets with it. network.ts:99 describes the group as 'Postgres — application tier only'.
findings.impact: All four conditions for internet reachability are established inside this tree: public IP, a subnet with an IGW default route, a security group permitting 0.0.0.0/0:5432, and a listening engine. A replica of the production database is directly reachable from the internet on the Postgres port, carrying the full contents of the primary. This enables credential brute-force against the master user and exploitation of any Postgres CVE with no network prerequisite. The rule silently contradicts the stated design in a different file, so a reviewer reading network.ts alone concludes the database is application-tier-only.
findings.recommendation: Delete the ingress rule; give the BI tool a dedicated security group referenced via referencedSecurityGroupId, or terminate it on a PrivateLink endpoint. Move replicaSubnets to network.privateSubnetIds and set publiclyAccessible: false. Do not mix a standalone SecurityGroupIngressRule with the inline ingress block at network.ts:100-107 — the provider treats inline rules as authoritative and will add and remove this rule on alternating runs.

triage.reason: No NACL, managed firewall or VPC endpoint policy is declared in this tree; an undeclared front-end firewall may not be assumed.
5432 is not the public-load-balancer case; that construct is edge.ts:76-77 and is different.

For the replica. The rule is attached to the shared dbSecurityGroup, and for the PRIMARY it is narrowed (publiclyAccessible:false at data.ts:47 plus private subnets whose route table has no default route). For the REPLICA nothing narrows it, and the finding stands on the replica.

scope.established_by: join of data.ts:63,64 (SG + public IP) with data.ts:55 -> network.ts:57 -> network.ts:53-56 -> network.ts:30-33 (IGW default route), plus the ingress rule; createDataTier is called unconditionally at index.ts:64 in both stacks
scope.narrowed_by: pulumi-platform/data.ts:47 and pulumi-platform/network.ts:38-41 — narrows the same SG rule for the primary instance only, not for the replica.

findings.title: /internal/* reaches the dispatch console without the OIDC authentication its /console/* sibling requires, and the rule that blocks the prefix is on a different web ACL
findings.class: Authentication bypass / broken access control (CWE-306, CWE-288)
findings.evidence: edge.ts:102-122 ListenerRule ${env}-rule-console, priority 20, pathPattern ['/console/*'], actions authenticate-oidc then forward to consoleTargetGroup. edge.ts:124-132 ListenerRule ${env}-rule-internal, priority 30, pathPattern ['/internal/*'], actions forward to the SAME consoleTargetGroup with no authentication action. The claimed compensating control does not reach the ALB: edge.ts:207-235 defines cdnAcl with `scope: 'CLOUDFRONT'` and rule block-internal-prefix matching '/internal/', attached only to reportsDistribution at edge.ts:239; the ALB is associated at edge.ts:192-195 with albAcl, whose single rule (edge.ts:159-189) matches '/ops/'.
findings.impact: Any unauthenticated internet client requesting https://<alb>/internal/<path> is forwarded to the dispatch console container with no identity established. edge.ts:100-101 states the console has no login of its own and the listener is the only authentication in front of it, so the entire staff console is reachable by changing one path segment. Each control is correct in isolation; the defect exists only in the join, which is why reading either file harder does not surface it.
findings.recommendation: Attach the same authenticate-oidc action to the internal rule, or delete the rule and give Grafana a machine-to-machine path that authenticates with a signed token at the console. If the prefix must stay, add an /internal/ block rule to albAcl restricted to the Grafana source.

triage.reason: The candidate compensating control is the WAF rule at edge.ts:218; it lives on cdnAcl (scope CLOUDFRONT) bound only to the distribution. A CLOUDFRONT-scope web ACL cannot be associated with an ALB at all.
createEdge is called unconditionally at index.ts:52 in both stacks; the rule is not behind any flag.
The forward is unconditional — no host-header or source condition narrows which callers may use it.

scope.established_by: targetGroupArn at edge.ts:131 identical to edge.ts:120; albAcl rule list enumerated at edge.ts:159-189; association targets read at edge.ts:193-194 and edge.ts:239

findings.title: Task-role S3 permissions granted on account-wide wildcard bucket ARNs, crossing both the tenant and the staging/prod boundary
findings.class: Over-permissive IAM resource scope (CWE-284, CWE-732)
findings.evidence: iam.ts:19-20 `Action: ['s3:GetObject','s3:PutObject'], Resource: 'arn:aws:s3:::*-reports/customer/*'`; iam.ts:31-32 `Action: ['s3:PutObject'], Resource: 'arn:aws:s3:::*-reports/*'`; iam.ts:38-39 `Action: ['s3:GetObject','s3:ListBucket'], Resource: ['arn:aws:s3:::*-exports','arn:aws:s3:::*-exports/*']`; iam.ts:24-25 `Resource: 'arn:aws:secretsmanager:*:*:secret:fieldops/api/*'`. None carries a Condition; the Statement type at iam.ts:4-9 makes Condition optional and no entry supplies one.
findings.impact: S3 bucket names are a single global namespace, so arn:aws:s3:::*-reports/* matches every bucket in every AWS account whose name ends in -reports. An attacker who creates attacker-reports in their own account receives writes from a compromised reports-renderer, with no egress policy stopping it. Both stacks deploy to the same region and account with names differing only by the -staging/-prod segment, so the staging fieldops-api role's grant matches the production reports bucket, and the secrets statement wildcards both the region and the account id. Secondary: aws.s3.BucketV2 is declared without a bucket property at storage.ts:28, 94, 136, so Pulumi auto-names the physical buckets with a random suffix and the grants reach foreign buckets while failing to reach this stack's own.
findings.recommendation: Replace every literal ARN with the Pulumi output of the bucket that is meant, built with pulumi.interpolate. Add Condition: { StringEquals: { 'aws:ResourceAccount': '${aws:PrincipalAccount}' } } to every S3 statement as a backstop. Scope the Secrets Manager ARN to the concrete account and region.

triage.reason: No SCP or resource-control policy in this tree; no bucket policy denies foreign principals — the reports bucket policy only adds an allow.
No comment or config claims the cross-account reach is intended; the naming pattern suggests the author believed the ARNs were stack-local.
No condition narrows the statements. The only narrowing anywhere near this is index.ts:72-84, which is additive rather than restrictive.

scope.established_by: the loop at iam.ts:65-88 attaches one RolePolicy per SERVICES entry; createRoles is called at index.ts:43 in both stacks

findings.title: The tenant-scoped loader policy is additive to the broad grant and names a bucket ARN that cannot match the auto-named bucket
findings.class: Ineffective access control / illusory least privilege (CWE-284, CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: index.ts:71-84 creates a RolePolicy documented as 'Scoped read on this tenant's own export objects', granting s3:GetObject on `arn:aws:s3:::${prefix}-exports/tenants/${tenantSlug}/*` to taskRoles['warehouse-loader']. The same role already carries iam.ts:38-39 `Resource: ['arn:aws:s3:::*-exports','arn:aws:s3:::*-exports/*']` from iam.ts:82. storage.ts:28 declares the bucket with no `bucket:` property, so Pulumi auto-names it with a random suffix.
findings.impact: The construct reads as the narrowing that makes the wildcard grant acceptable and is not one, for two independent reasons. IAM takes the union of allows across two differently-named inline policies on the same role, so the broad *-exports/* grant is untouched and the loader still reads every tenant's objects. And the hardcoded ARN matches nothing, because the physical bucket name carries a random suffix. The statement grants zero additional access while creating the appearance of tenant isolation.
findings.recommendation: Delete the wildcard statement at iam.ts:38-39 and make this the only export grant, built from storage.exports.arn via pulumi.interpolate. If tenant isolation is a real requirement, enforce it with an s3:prefix condition and a bucket policy Deny for anything outside the tenant prefix.

triage.reason: It is exactly what it looks like syntactically — an aws.iam.RolePolicy. What it is not is what its own docstring at index.ts:71 claims: a scope.
This is not defence in depth that happens to be absent; it is the primary tenant-isolation control named in the code, and it is inert.
FP-11 asks whether a wide construct applies to less than it reads. This is the inverse: a narrow construct that narrows nothing.

scope.established_by: role target read at index.ts:73 matched to iam.ts:87 taskRoles['warehouse-loader']; IAM inline-policy union semantics; absence of a bucket property at storage.ts:28

findings.title: The partner analytics role reads the entire reports bucket, including the internal/ prefix the CDN goes out of its way to block
findings.class: Broken access control / third-party over-grant (CWE-284, CWE-732)
findings.evidence: storage.ts:111-113 comments that the partner analytics job reads the objects directly rather than through the distribution. storage.ts:123-127 `Sid:'PartnerDirectRead', Principal:{ AWS: partner }, Action:['s3:GetObject','s3:ListBucket'], Resource: [arn, `${arn}/*`]`. edge.ts:205-206 declares anything under internal/ staff-only and edge.ts:216-227 blocks '/internal/' at the CloudFront edge. iam.ts:99-104 makes the partner role assumable by `Principal: { AWS: '*' }` gated only on sts:ExternalId and aws:SecureTransport.
findings.impact: The code declares internal/ staff-only and blocks it at the CloudFront edge, then grants a third party s3:GetObject on the whole bucket over a path the edge does not sit on — the comment says so explicitly. The WAF rule is a control on a route the privileged reader never takes. The reach extends: the trust policy has no aws:PrincipalAccount or aws:PrincipalOrgID alongside the external ID, and that external ID is defined in no stack file in this repository, so its entropy cannot be verified here.
findings.recommendation: Scope the statement to the published prefix with an s3:prefix condition on ListBucket, and add an explicit Deny on `${arn}/internal/*` for any principal other than the renderer role. Add aws:PrincipalOrgID or the partner's concrete account id to the trust policy. Move the staff-only material to a separate bucket — a prefix is the wrong boundary for two audiences.

triage.reason: The candidate control is the WAF rule at edge.ts:218, which applies to CloudFront requests; storage.ts:112-113 states the partner deliberately bypasses the distribution.
The partner read is intended and bounded to rendered reports; the grant is not bounded to them. Per FP-05 the finding moves to the internal/ prefix behind the intended exposure.
storage.ts:95 tags the bucket Contains: 'rendered-customer-reports', and edge.ts:206 classifies the internal/ prefix as staff-only working material.
Resource is [arn, `${arn}/*`] with no prefix condition; the construct is exactly as wide as it reads.

scope.established_by: partnerRoleArn traced index.ts:43 -> index.ts:49 -> storage.ts:11 -> storage.ts:117,125; the reports BucketPolicy is unconditional, so it applies in both stacks
scope.narrowed_by: pulumi-platform/iam.ts:102 — sts:ExternalId narrows WHO can assume the role, not WHAT the role may read once assumed.

findings.title: The ALB forwards unvalidated request headers and the architecture treats x-fieldops-* headers as a client-certificate identity
findings.class: Authentication bypass by header spoofing / request smuggling (CWE-290, CWE-444)
findings.evidence: edge.ts:32-35 sets `dropInvalidHeaderFields: false` with a comment stating that the dispatcher fleet's client-certificate identity reaches the ALB as a set of x-fieldops-* headers 'so the listener has to pass request headers through to the target group untouched'. edge.ts:92-98 forwards /api/* with no header manipulation. albAcl (edge.ts:151-190) has one rule, matching '/ops/'; nothing removes or overwrites x-fieldops-*.
findings.impact: Two defects share this line. dropInvalidHeaderFields: false makes the ALB forward headers containing characters outside the valid set, the precondition for header-parsing desynchronisation between the load balancer and the backend. And the comment documents the higher-value problem: an mTLS identity carried as an ordinary request header on a listener open to 0.0.0.0/0, with nothing stripping it on inbound requests. Inference not closed: whether the API actually trusts those headers — the application code is a different component, and the fieldops-api audit found the corresponding trusted-proxy path at auth.ts:46.
findings.recommendation: Set dropInvalidHeaderFields: true. Do not carry identity in a client-settable header: terminate mTLS at the ALB and use the x-amzn-mtls-clientcert* headers the ALB itself injects and overwrites, or verify a signed assertion in the API. As an interim control, add a WAF rule blocking any request presenting an x-fieldops-* header from outside the dispatcher range.

triage.reason: The API may verify a signed token independently of the headers — edge.ts:92 claims 'the API authenticates its own callers'. That is a claim inside audited content, not evidence. Caps the finding at probable.
Request headers on a listener whose security group admits 0.0.0.0/0 (network.ts:76) are attacker-controlled by definition.
dropInvalidHeaderFields is a load-balancer attribute; it applies to every listener and every target group on this ALB, not to one route.

scope.established_by: attribute set on the LoadBalancer resource itself; the four ListenerRules at edge.ts:93,102,127,136 all sit behind it

findings.title: Two aws.s3.BucketPolicy resources target the same bucket in staging, making the effective policy non-deterministic
findings.class: Non-deterministic security control (CWE-1188)
findings.evidence: storage.ts:50-51 `if (args.publicExports) { new aws.s3.BucketPolicy(`${env}-exports-policy`, { bucket: exports_.id, ... })` and storage.ts:70-73 `if (args.replicateProdExports) { new aws.s3.BucketPolicy(`${env}-exports-replication-policy`, { bucket: exports_.id, ... })`. Pulumi.staging.yaml:9 and :12 set both flags true; Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8 sets both false.
findings.impact: S3 permits exactly one policy document per bucket. Two Pulumi resources both writing PutBucketPolicy to the same bucket resolve last-writer-wins with no dependency ordering declared, so which grant survives depends on the provider's execution order and flips between runs. The security posture of a bucket holding billing exports is undefined by the code: on one apply the bucket is anonymously readable, on the next it accepts prod replication and is not.
findings.recommendation: Build one policy document with both statement sets and create a single BucketPolicy. Add a CI assertion that no two BucketPolicy resources share a bucket argument.

triage.reason: Both are genuinely aws.s3.BucketPolicy resources with the same bucket argument (storage.ts:52 and storage.ts:74). There is no reading that makes this benign.
Narrowed to the staging stack only: the conflict requires both flags true, which is Pulumi.staging.yaml:9 and :12. In prod neither block executes and no policy is created at all.

scope.established_by: both if-blocks evaluated against Pulumi.staging.yaml:9,12 and Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8 via index.ts:13-14,47-48
scope.narrowed_by: pulumi-platform/Pulumi.prod.yaml:7-8 — the prod stack creates neither resource, so the conflict is staging-only.

findings.title: Deletion protection on the production load balancer can never be enabled: the comparison is against a value that is always a prefix
findings.class: Dead control / availability (CWE-1188, CWE-665)
findings.evidence: index.ts:11 `const env = cfg.require('environment')` ('prod'); index.ts:38-39 `const tenantSlug = slug(tenant); const prefix = `${tenantSlug}-${env}``; index.ts:52-53 `createEdge({ env: prefix, ... })`. Inside createEdge, env is 'acme-utilities-north-prod', so edge.ts:31 `enableDeletionProtection: env === 'prod'` is false in every stack. The same substitution reaches createNetwork, createRoles, createStorage and createDataTier; edge.ts:31 is the only place a module compares it to a bare environment name.
findings.impact: A guard that cannot fire. The production ALB — the single ingress for the API and the dispatch console — is deletable by any principal with elasticloadbalancing:DeleteLoadBalancer, including the settlement-worker administrator role. The code reads as though prod is protected, so the gap is invisible on review. Note the asymmetry with the data tier, where deletionProtection: true is set literally at data.ts:46 and does work.
findings.recommendation: Pass the raw environment alongside the prefix and compare against that, or set enableDeletionProtection: true unconditionally. Add a unit assertion that the prod stack renders it true.

triage.reason: createEdge runs in both stacks unconditionally (index.ts:52); this is the shipped path, not a debug branch.
It is the only deletion control on this resource, not a redundant layer.
The construct is narrower than intended, not wider; FP-11 addresses the opposite direction.

scope.established_by: value of env inside createEdge traced from index.ts:11 -> index.ts:39 -> index.ts:53 -> edge.ts:25

findings.title: The footprint declares no audit logging of any kind, and ALB access logs are directed at a bucket the program never creates
findings.class: Missing security logging and monitoring (CWE-778)
findings.evidence: edge.ts:36 `accessLogs: { bucket: `${env}-alb-logs`, enabled: true }`. `grep -rn "alb-logs"` returns that line and nothing else — no BucketV2, no log-delivery bucket policy. `grep -rniE "flowlog|cloudtrail|loggingConfig|enabledCloudwatchLogsExports|logging"` over the scope returns zero. Absent resource by resource: aws.ec2.FlowLog on the VPC, loggingConfig on the distribution, enabledCloudwatchLogsExports on either RDS instance, any cloudtrail.Trail, any BucketLogging, any alarm. The only telemetry declared is WAF sampled requests and log_min_duration_statement on the primary.
findings.impact: Every other finding here becomes undetectable and unreconstructable: no record of who assumed the partner role, what the administrator role did, which anonymous clients read the staging exports bucket, or which sources connected to the internet-facing replica. The ALB access-log configuration compounds it — enabled: true against a bucket that does not exist means either the load balancer fails to create or logging silently never delivers.
findings.recommendation: Create the alb-logs bucket with the ELB log-delivery policy. Add FlowLog on the VPC with trafficType ALL, loggingConfig on the distribution, enabledCloudwatchLogsExports on both RDS instances, and an organization-level CloudTrail with log-file integrity validation. Add metric filters and alarms for IAM policy changes and PutBucketPolicy.

triage.reason: Logging may be centralised in a security account by a landing zone outside this repository; the exculpation requires written evidence and none exists in this tree. The alb-logs half is not affected — the bucket is named by this program and absent from this program.
Detection is load-bearing here: the account contains an administrator role and an internet-facing database.

scope.established_by: inventory of every data-bearing and network resource in the scope, subtracted from a grep for logging constructs across all ten files (zero hits)

findings.title: Staging and production deploy into the same region with no account, provider or state separation declared, while IAM grants span both by wildcard
findings.class: Environment separation / trust boundary (CWE-668)
findings.evidence: Pulumi.prod.yaml:2 and Pulumi.staging.yaml:2 both set `aws:region: us-east-2`; both set the identical tenant at line 5. index.ts:41 passes the identical CIDR '10.0.0.0/16' to createNetwork in both stacks. Neither stack file declares aws:profile, aws:assumeRole, aws:accessKey or any account discriminator, and Pulumi.yaml:10-18 declares no such template key. The only difference between the two environments is the -staging/-prod segment of the resource-name prefix.
findings.impact: With no account boundary, the wildcards cross environments inside one blast radius: arn:aws:s3:::*-reports/* held by a staging role matches the production reports bucket, and arn:aws:secretsmanager:*:*:secret:fieldops/api/* matches production secrets. This is the mechanism that turns the staging-only exposures — the world-readable exports bucket and the internet-facing replica — into a production incident. Both stacks also use 10.0.0.0/16, so the two VPCs can never be peered. Inference not closed: Pulumi credentials may be supplied per-stack from the environment or from ESC outside these files.
findings.recommendation: Deploy each stack into a separate AWS account and pin it in the stack file. Give the environments distinct VPC CIDRs. Independently of the account decision, remove the wildcards so the separation does not rest on account isolation alone.

triage.reason: Per-stack credentials may be injected by the deployment platform or by Pulumi ESC; the exculpation requires the artifact and none is present. Caps the finding at probable.
These are root stack configuration files, not a reusable module — Pulumi.yaml:1-5 declares the project and runtime.
The staging/prod difference is name-prefix only; nothing in either file narrows the account or region.

scope.established_by: key-by-key comparison of the two stack files (eleven keys each) plus a grep for any account-selecting provider key across all three YAML files

findings.title: Four configuration names are read by the program and defined by nothing in the project; three are secrets
findings.class: Undefined configuration / unverifiable secret (CWE-1188, CWE-522)
findings.evidence: index.ts:20-23 read dbMasterPassword, oidcClientSecret and partnerExternalId with requireSecret, and certificateArn with require. The subtraction run both ways: thirteen names are read across index.ts (lines 11-23, 56-57, 95); eleven are defined in each stack file. Neither stack file contains an encryptionsalt or secretsprovider line, which is the artifact Pulumi writes the first time a secret is set on a stack.

The impact is different and still real: partnerExternalId is the sole control narrowing Principal:{AWS:'*'} at iam.ts:99-104, and its value, length and rotation state cannot be established from this repository at all. Specify a minimum length and a rotation owner for partnerExternalId, and reference dbMasterPassword from Secrets Manager with managed rotation.

index.ts is the program entrypoint (package.json:5); these reads execute on every preview and every up.

The four may be injected by a deployment platform or by Pulumi ESC; without the exported artifact the answer is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS. It caps the finding at probable and is precisely why it is written down rather than dropped.
No prefix loader or wholesale config struct is in use; each name is read individually through the pulumi.Config API.

scope.established_by: list of names read (thirteen distinct) minus list of names defined (eleven per stack file)

findings.title: The reports bucket permits public bucket policies and cross-account access by policy
findings.class: Weakened object-storage guardrail (CWE-668)
findings.evidence: storage.ts:98-104 `new aws.s3.BucketPublicAccessBlock(`${env}-reports-pab`, { bucket: reports.id, blockPublicAcls: true, blockPublicPolicy: false, ignorePublicAcls: true, restrictPublicBuckets: false })` — hard-coded asymmetrically, not driven by a config flag, in both stacks.
findings.impact: The two ACL flags are on and the two policy flags are off, exactly the combination that lets a public Principal:'*' policy be attached to the bucket holding rendered customer reports, including the internal/ staff-only prefix. restrictPublicBuckets: false additionally permits cross-account principals to use the bucket through its policy — which is how the partner grant works today, meaning the guardrail was disabled deliberately for that grant. The control that would stop the next BucketPolicy from being public is switched off. No versioning is configured on this bucket either, unlike exports.

findings.class: Non-reproducible dependency resolution (CWE-1104, CWE-1357)
findings.evidence: Thirty declared dependencies enumerated by hand: 18 Node specifiers, all caret (fieldops-api/package.json:14-24 and pulumi-platform/package.json:12-18); 10 Python specifiers, all unbounded >= with no ceiling (atlas-rag/pyproject.toml:7-12 and settlement-worker/pyproject.toml:7-11); 8 Gradle coordinates, all exact. A find over the whole tree returns zero lockfiles of any kind — no package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, uv.lock, poetry.lock, requirements*.txt or gradle.lockfile — and no .npmrc, pip.conf, packageManager field, overrides or resolutions block.
findings.impact: Two installs of the same commit are not the same artifact, and a compromised minor or patch of any of the 28 floating packages is adopted automatically at the next install with no integrity check. The Python side is worse than the Node side: a caret bounds a major, >= does not. This matters concretely here: the pulumi program's dependency graph executes inside the process that holds AWS deploy credentials — the widest credential in the system — and two findings elsewhere in this report turn on framework behaviour that cannot be pinned to a reviewed version without a lock. Inference not closed: an internal proxy or registry could freeze versions, and no CI file, .npmrc or registry config exists in the tree to establish it.
findings.recommendation: Commit a lockfile per component and install from it (npm ci, uv sync --frozen); add ceilings to the ten unbounded Python specifiers; add a pinned build backend to both pyproject files; for Gradle add dependency verification metadata since the coordinates are already exact. Add a composition-analysis step to CI — the only script in either package.json today is a type check.

triage.reason: No compensating control: no overrides block, no verification metadata, no vendored dependencies anywhere in the tree.

The usual exculpation is an internal proxy or registry freezing versions, and that requires the exported artifact. There is no CI file, no .npmrc and no registry config in the tree, so no evidence arrived. Caps the finding at probable.
All four manifests are applications (private: true, console entry points, a Pulumi program), not publishable libraries, so the 'library resolves on the consumer side' reading does not apply.
Not defence in depth — the resolution is the artifact.

scope.established_by: hand enumeration of all 30 specifiers plus a find sweep for every lockfile name in the four ecosystems
scope.narrowed_by: atlas-android/app/build.gradle.kts:72 — the eight Android coordinates are exactly pinned and are excluded from this finding.
